title: Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction and Polarization

toc.title: 13.1 Coherent sources and the conditions for interference; Young's double-slit experiment
13.2 Diffraction at a single slit and at a grating; resolving power of optical instruments

html:
Light behaves as a wave in three experiments that no particle model explains: two beams that add to darkness (interference), light that spreads into the shadow of an edge (diffraction), and light that refuses to pass through two crossed sheets (polarization).

The Waves and Optics area carries 8 of the 50 Physics questions, with about 2 questions from this chapter — usually one numerical on a fringe or a slit and one short conceptual item.

The whole chapter turns on a single question asked at a point on a screen: what is the path difference here, and is it a whole number of wavelengths?

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • What makes two sources coherent, and the two ways of producing coherent beams (wavefront and amplitude).
  • The interference conditions: path difference n\lambda for bright, (2n-1)\lambda/2 for dark; and \phi = 2\pi\Delta/\lambda.
  • Young's double slit: \beta = \lambda D/d, its three proportionalities, \beta in a liquid, and the shift made by a slab.
  • Intensity: I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi and I_{max}/I_{min} = (a_1+a_2)^2/(a_1-a_2)^2.
  • Single slit: minima at a\sin\theta = n\lambda; central maximum width 2D\lambda/a.
  • Grating: (a+b)\sin\theta = n\lambda; how many orders fit; resolving power of a telescope and a microscope.
  • Malus's law I = I_0\cos^2\theta; Brewster's law \tan\theta_p = \mu; why reflected light is partly polarized.

13.1 Coherent sources and the conditions for interference; Young's double-slit experiment

13.1.1 Superposition, and what interference actually is

When two waves reach the same point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the two displacements. The waves pass through one another and separate again unchanged.

What we see on a screen is not the displacement but the intensity, which is proportional to the square of the resultant amplitude:

I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi

where I_1 and I_2 are the intensities the waves would have separately and \phi is the phase difference between them at that point. Three cases matter:

Phase difference Path difference Intensity Name
0, 2\pi, 4\pi, \dots 0, \lambda, 2\lambda, \dots (\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2})^2, maximum constructive
\pi, 3\pi, 5\pi, \dots \lambda/2, 3\lambda/2, \dots (\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2})^2, minimum destructive
\pi/2 \lambda/4 I_1 + I_2 neither

For two equal sources, I_1 = I_2 = I_0: the maximum is 4I_0 (not 2I_0 — amplitudes add, and 2^2 = 4) and the minimum is exactly zero.

Energy is not destroyed; it is redistributed from the dark fringes into the bright ones, and the average intensity over the pattern is still 2I_0.

Adding intensities is wrong

Two identical lamps lighting a wall give 2I. Two coherent beams of the same intensity give 4I at a bright fringe and 0 at a dark one. Whenever a question says "coherent", add amplitudes first and then square; never add intensities unless the sources are incoherent.

The contrast of a pattern is measured by its visibility,

V = \frac{I_{max} - I_{min}}{I_{max} + I_{min}}

which is 1 for equal amplitudes and falls as the amplitudes become unequal. Writing the amplitude ratio as a_1/a_2,

\frac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left(\frac{a_1+a_2}{a_1-a_2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}}\right)^2

This one formula generates a whole family of paper questions, and the trap is always the same: an intensity ratio must be square-rooted before it is put into the amplitude formula.

13.1.2 Coherent sources

Coherent sources

Two sources are coherent if they emit waves of the same frequency whose phase difference at any point remains constant in time. Only then is the interference pattern stationary and visible.

Two independent lamps, even two identical sodium lamps, are not coherent.

Each atom emits a wave train lasting about 10^{-8} s, and the phase of the next train is random; the pattern from one pair of trains is wiped out by the next, long before the eye or a photographic plate can record it.

A laser is different: stimulated emission keeps the phase fixed over a coherence length of metres, so two beams from one laser interfere easily.

Since independent sources will not do, one source must be split and the two parts recombined. There are two ways:

Method What is divided Examples
Division of wavefront one wavefront is cut into two parts by slits, mirrors or a prism Young's double slit, Fresnel biprism, Lloyd's mirror
Division of amplitude one beam is partly reflected and partly transmitted at a surface thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson interferometer

13.1.3 The conditions for sustained interference

For a pattern that can be seen and measured, all of the following must hold:

  1. The two sources must be coherent — same frequency, constant phase difference.
  2. They must have the same wavelength (monochromatic light gives clean fringes).
  3. Their amplitudes must be comparable; if one beam is much weaker the minima are only slightly darker than the maxima and the fringes are washed out.
  4. The two waves must have the same (or nearly the same) plane of polarization; perpendicularly polarized beams do not interfere at all.
  5. The source must be narrow. A wide source behaves as many independent point sources whose patterns are displaced from one another and overlap into uniform brightness.
  6. The path difference must be within the coherence length of the light; beyond it the phase relationship is lost.

13.1.4 Path difference and phase difference

A path difference \Delta means one wave has travelled a distance \Delta further than the other. One whole wavelength corresponds to a phase change of 2\pi, so

\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\Delta \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Delta = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi}\,\phi

Path difference \Delta Phase difference \phi Result with equal sources
0 0 bright, 4I_0
\lambda/4 \pi/2 2I_0
\lambda/2 \pi dark, zero
3\lambda/4 3\pi/2 2I_0
n\lambda 2n\pi bright
(2n-1)\lambda/2 (2n-1)\pi dark

Optical path. In a medium of refractive index \mu the wavelength is \lambda/\mu while the frequency is unchanged, so the same geometrical distance contains \mu times as many wavelengths.

The optical path is \mu \times (geometrical path), and it is optical paths that are compared when the two beams pass through different media.

13.1.5 Young's double slit: where the fringes come from

A single slit S is placed in front of two narrow slits S_1 and S_2 a distance d apart, and a screen stands a distance D beyond them, with D \gg d. Light from S reaches S_1 and S_2 in phase, so they act as two coherent sources.

At a point P on the screen, at distance y from the centre O, the two beams have travelled slightly different distances and interfere.

Fringe width in Young's double slit

We start from the geometry of the two paths and want the spacing between neighbouring bright fringes.

Setting up. Slits S_1, S_2 separated by d; screen at distance D \gg d; P at height y above the centre O.

Step 1 — write the two path lengths by Pythagoras.

S_2P^2 = D^2 + \left(y + \frac{d}{2}\right)^2, \qquad S_1P^2 = D^2 + \left(y - \frac{d}{2}\right)^2

Step 2 — subtract, so that D^2 cancels.

S_2P^2 - S_1P^2 = \left(y + \frac{d}{2}\right)^2 - \left(y - \frac{d}{2}\right)^2 = 2yd

Step 3 — factor the left side.

(S_2P - S_1P)(S_2P + S_1P) = 2yd

Step 4 — use D \gg d and D \gg y, so that S_2P + S_1P \approx 2D. Then

\Delta = S_2P - S_1P = \frac{2yd}{2D} = \frac{yd}{D}

Step 5 — bright fringes need \Delta = n\lambda.

\frac{y_n d}{D} = n\lambda \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y_n = \frac{n\lambda D}{d}

Step 6 — the spacing is the difference between consecutive orders.

\beta = y_{n+1} - y_n = \frac{(n+1)\lambda D}{d} - \frac{n\lambda D}{d} = \frac{\lambda D}{d}

Result.

\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}

What it means. Every bright fringe is the same distance \beta from the next — the pattern is a comb of equally spaced lines. \beta grows with \lambda and D and shrinks as the slits are moved apart.

The result assumes D \gg d, small angles (\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta \approx \theta), a monochromatic coherent source and one medium throughout.

Key writing criteria

The Pythagoras step, the difference-of-squares factorisation, and the explicit approximation S_2P + S_1P \approx 2D. Write the reason for the approximation in words; that sentence usually carries a mark.

Quantity Formula
Position of the nth bright fringe y_n = n\lambda D/d, n = 0, 1, 2, \dots
Position of the nth dark fringe y_n = (2n-1)\lambda D/d, n = 1, 2, \dots
Fringe width \beta = \lambda D/d
Angular fringe width \theta = \lambda/d
Path difference at P \Delta = yd/D

The central fringe (n = 0) is bright because the paths are equal. The first dark fringe is at half a fringe width from the centre, the first bright fringe at one full fringe width.

13.1.6 What changes the fringe width — and what does not

Change made Effect on \beta Reason
Longer wavelength (red instead of violet) increases \beta \propto \lambda
Screen moved further away increases \beta \propto D
Slits moved further apart decreases \beta \propto 1/d
Whole apparatus immersed in a liquid of index \mu falls to \beta/\mu \lambda_{liquid} = \lambda/\mu
A slab of thickness t, index \mu, over one slit unchanged; the pattern shifts by (\mu-1)t/\beta fringes towards that slit extra optical path (\mu-1)t
White light instead of monochromatic central fringe white, coloured fringes either side, red outermost \beta \propto \lambda
One slit covered fringes disappear, only a broad diffraction pattern remains one source only
Order n of the fringe no effect \beta is independent of n

Why the pattern shifts with a slab. The slab adds (\mu-1)t to the optical path of one beam.

To bring the paths back to equality the point P must move towards the covered slit, so the whole pattern — including the white central fringe — moves that way.

The number of fringes through which it moves is the extra optical path divided by one fringe width.

Three traps in one formula
  1. \beta \propto 1/d, not 1/d^2 and not 1/D.
  2. Immersing the apparatus in water changes \lambda, not the frequency, and not D or d; so \beta falls by the factor \mu — it does not rise.
  3. The fringe width is unchanged by a slab; only the position of the pattern moves. Many students wrongly say the fringes get wider.
Worked example 13.1 — fringe width, in air and in water

Problem. Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on two slits 0.5 mm apart; the screen is 1.0 m away. Find the fringe width. What does it become if the whole set-up is immersed in water of refractive index 4/3?

Solution. \beta = \lambda D/d = (600\times10^{-9})(1.0)/(0.5\times10^{-3}) = 1.2\times10^{-3} m = 1.2 mm. In water \lambda' = 600/1.333 = 450 nm, so \beta' = \beta/\mu = 1.2/(4/3) = 0.9 mm.

The frequency is unchanged; only the wavelength in the medium matters.

Worked example 13.2 — shift produced by a glass sheet

Problem. In a double-slit experiment \beta = 0.1 mm. A glass sheet 0.2 mm thick and of refractive index 1.5 is placed in front of one slit. Through how many fringes does the pattern shift, and in which direction?

Solution. Extra optical path = (\mu-1)t = 0.5\times0.2 = 0.1 mm. Number of fringes = 0.1/0.1 = 1. The pattern shifts by one fringe towards the covered slit, because that beam has been delayed.

Worked example 13.3 — intensity ratio from an intensity ratio

Problem. Two coherent beams of intensities I and 4I interfere. Find I_{max}/I_{min}.

Solution. Amplitudes are proportional to \sqrt{I}, so a_1:a_2 = 1:2. Then I_{max}/I_{min} = (3/1)^2 = 9.

Answer 9 1. Note that the intensity ratio 1 : 4 becomes an amplitude ratio 1 : 2 before it is used — the commonest slip is to write (4+1)/(4-1).

13.1.7 Thin films and Newton's rings

A soap film or a thin oil slick shows coloured bands in daylight. The two interfering beams here are the reflection from the top surface and the reflection from the bottom surface of the film, so this is division of amplitude.

For a film of thickness t and refractive index \mu, with light travelling at angle r inside the film, the second beam covers a distance 2t/\cos r in the film; but the extra optical path, measured between wavefronts of the two emerging rays, works out to 2\mu t\cos r (the \cos r appears because the rays leave along the same direction).

In addition, the reflection at the top surface is from a denser medium (air to film), which changes the phase by \pi, equivalent to an extra \lambda/2. Hence

\Delta = 2\mu t\cos r + \frac{\lambda}{2}

Reflected light from a film in air Condition
Bright 2\mu t\cos r = (2n-1)\lambda/2
Dark 2\mu t\cos r = n\lambda

At near-normal incidence \cos r \approx 1. This is why a soap film appears black just before it bursts: as t \to 0 the condition 2\mu t = 0 = n\lambda with n = 0 is a dark condition.

Anti-reflection coating. A coating whose refractive index lies between those of air and glass gives a \pi phase change at both surfaces, so the two shifts cancel. Destruction then needs 2\mu t = \lambda/2, i.e. t = \lambda/(4\mu) — a quarter-wavelength layer.

Newton's rings. A plano-convex lens of radius of curvature R rests on a flat glass plate, trapping a thin air film whose thickness at radius r is t = r^2/(2R). With \mu = 1 and normal incidence:

Feature (reflected light) Result
Centre dark, because t = 0 gives the dark condition
Dark rings r_n = \sqrt{n\lambda R}, n = 1, 2, 3, \dots (the centre is n = 0)
Bright rings r_n = \sqrt{(2n-1)\lambda R/2}, n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
Spacing rings crowd together as r grows, since r \propto \sqrt{n}
In transmitted light centre bright, pattern complementary to the reflected one
Gap filled with liquid of index \mu rings shrink, r \propto 1/\sqrt{\mu}
Worked example 13.4 — radius of a Newton's ring

Problem. A plano-convex lens of radius of curvature 1.0 m rests on a glass plate and is viewed in reflected light of wavelength 600 nm. Find the radius of the third dark ring.

Solution. r_3 = \sqrt{3\lambda R} = \sqrt{3(600\times10^{-9})(1.0)} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-6}} = 1.34\times10^{-3} m = 1.34 mm.

13.2 Diffraction at a single slit and at a grating; resolving power of optical instruments

13.2.1 What diffraction is

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes an obstacle or an aperture, so that light appears inside the geometrical shadow. It becomes noticeable when the size of the obstacle or slit is comparable with the wavelength.

Sound bends round doorways easily because its wavelength is about a metre; light does not noticeably bend round a door because its wavelength is a fraction of a micrometre — but round a razor edge or through a narrow slit the fringes are clear.

Fresnel diffraction Fraunhofer diffraction
Source and screen at finite distances effectively at infinity (lenses used)
Wavefronts at the aperture spherical or cylindrical plane
Treatment complicated simple; the standard school case

13.2.2 Single slit: where the minima fall

Let parallel rays fall on a slit of width a. Consider the secondary wavelets leaving the slit at angle \theta to the straight-through direction. The ray from the top edge and the ray from the bottom edge differ in path by a\sin\theta.

The first minimum. Divide the slit into two halves. The ray from the top edge and the ray from the centre of the slit differ by \frac{a}{2}\sin\theta. If that equals \lambda/2, each pair of points (one in each half) cancels, and the whole slit cancels itself:

\frac{a}{2}\sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad a\sin\theta = \lambda

The same pairing argument, with the slit divided into 2n parts, gives the nth minimum:

a\sin\theta = n\lambda, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots

Between the minima lie secondary maxima, approximately at

a\sin\theta = (2n+1)\frac{\lambda}{2}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots

but they are much weaker than the central maximum, and their exact positions are slightly displaced from this formula.

Minima here, maxima there

For a single slit, a\sin\theta = n\lambda gives minima (dark). For a double slit or grating, d\sin\theta = n\lambda gives maxima (bright).

The same-looking equation describes opposite things, because in the single slit the n\lambda is the path difference between the two edges of one slit, while in the grating it is between corresponding points of two neighbouring slits.

Examiners build a distractor on exactly this swap.

13.2.3 The central maximum

The first minimum is at \sin\theta_1 = \lambda/a, so for small angles \theta_1 \approx \lambda/a. The central maximum therefore has

Quantity Value
Angular half-width \theta_1 = \lambda/a
Full angular width 2\lambda/a
Linear width on a screen at distance D 2D\lambda/a
Width of each secondary maximum D\lambda/a (half the central one)

So the central maximum is twice as wide as any secondary maximum and far brighter. A narrower slit (a smaller) gives a wider central maximum — the opposite of what the word "narrow" suggests, and a favourite question.

Worked example 13.5 — width of the central maximum

Problem. Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through a slit 0.2 mm wide and falls on a screen 1.0 m away. Find the width of the central maximum.

Solution. 2D\lambda/a = 2(1.0)(600\times10^{-9})/(0.2\times10^{-3}) = 6.0\times10^{-3} m = 6 mm. The half-width, 3 mm, is the distance to the first minimum.

13.2.4 Interference and diffraction compared

Interference Diffraction
Origin two separate coherent sources secondary wavelets from different parts of one wavefront
Fringe widths all equal central maximum twice as wide as the others
Intensity of maxima equal, if the sources are equally bright falls off rapidly away from the centre
Minima perfectly dark for equal amplitudes not perfectly dark
Number of fringes few, and they are broad many, crowding together

13.2.5 The diffraction grating

A grating is a plate ruled with N parallel slits per metre. The distance between the centres of neighbouring slits is the grating element

d = a + b = \frac{1}{N}

where a is the slit width and b the opaque width. Parallel rays diffracted at angle \theta from neighbouring slits differ in path by d\sin\theta, and they add in phase when

(a+b)\sin\theta = n\lambda, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots

n is the order of the spectrum; n = 0 is the central white image. Because hundreds of slits contribute, the maxima are extremely sharp and bright (intensity proportional to N^2) while the space between them is almost dark.

That is why a grating, not a double slit, is used to measure wavelengths.

How many orders fit. Since \sin\theta cannot exceed 1,

n_{max} = \frac{d}{\lambda}

rounded down to a whole number. The highest order appears on each side of the centre, so the total number of principal maxima is 2n_{max} + 1 including the central one.

Missing orders. If d/a is a whole number, the diffraction minimum of each individual slit falls on the n = d/a interference maximum and that order is missing.

Worked example 13.6 — orders from a grating

Problem. A grating has 5000 lines per cm and is used with light of wavelength 500 nm. Find the grating element and the highest order visible.

Solution. d = 1/(5000\ \text{cm}^{-1}) = 1/(5\times10^{5}\ \text{m}^{-1}) = 2\times10^{-6} m. n_{max} = d/\lambda = 2\times10^{-6}/500\times10^{-9} = 4. Orders 1 to 4 appear on each side, so 9 principal maxima are seen in all.

13.2.6 Resolving power of optical instruments

Two stars, or two nearby points of a specimen, are not point images: each is spread by diffraction into a disc with a ring around it. The Rayleigh criterion says they are just resolved when the centre of one diffraction pattern falls on the first minimum of the other.

Instrument Limit of resolution Resolving power
Telescope (objective diameter D) \theta_{min} = 1.22\lambda/D D/(1.22\lambda)
Microscope (numerical aperture \mu\sin\theta) d_{min} = \lambda/(2\mu\sin\theta) 2\mu\sin\theta/\lambda
Grating (N lines, order n) — nN

For the telescope, only the diameter of the objective matters — not its focal length, not the magnification. A larger objective collects more light and resolves finer detail, which is why research telescopes are built large.

For the microscope, the numerical aperture \text{NA} = \mu\sin\theta is what counts; immersion oil raises \mu from 1 to about 1.5 and so improves resolution by that factor.

Some books quote the same limit in Rayleigh's form, 0.61\lambda/(\mu\sin\theta); use whichever form the numbers in the question fit.

Worked example 13.7 — resolution of a telescope

Problem. A telescope has an objective of diameter 10 cm and is used at wavelength 600 nm. What is the smallest angular separation it can resolve?

Solution. \theta_{min} = 1.22\lambda/D = 1.22(600\times10^{-9})/(0.10) = 7.3\times10^{-6} rad. Doubling the diameter would halve this angle.

13.3 Polarization and Brewster's law

13.3.1 Unpolarized and plane-polarized light

Light is a transverse wave: the electric field oscillates perpendicular to the direction of travel.

In unpolarized light the direction of that oscillation changes at random from instant to instant, so on average all directions across the beam are equally represented.

In plane-polarized light the electric field is confined to one plane containing the ray.

  • The plane of vibration is the plane containing the electric vector and the ray.
  • The plane of polarization is perpendicular to the plane of vibration and also contains the ray.

Only transverse waves can be polarized. Sound, a longitudinal wave, cannot be, and this is the experimental proof that light is transverse — a fact that interference and diffraction alone cannot establish.

13.3.2 How light is polarized

Method What happens
Selective absorption a Polaroid absorbs the component along its long molecular chains and transmits the perpendicular one
Reflection at one particular angle (Brewster's) the reflected beam is completely polarized
Refraction a pile of glass plates transmits a beam that is partially, and after many plates almost completely, polarized
Scattering light scattered at 90° by air molecules is strongly polarized
Double refraction calcite splits a beam into ordinary and extraordinary rays, polarized at right angles

A Polaroid is a sheet of aligned long-chain molecules. Light with its electric vector along the chains drives electrons along them and is absorbed; light perpendicular to the chains passes.

The first sheet is called the polarizer, the second (used to examine the light) the analyser.

13.3.3 Malus's law

If plane-polarized light of intensity I_0 falls on an analyser whose transmission axis makes an angle \theta with the plane of polarization, the transmitted intensity is

I = I_0\cos^2\theta

The transmitted beam remains plane-polarized, with its plane along the analyser's axis.

Situation Transmitted intensity
Unpolarized light I_0 through one Polaroid I_0/2
Plane-polarized I_0 through an analyser at \theta I_0\cos^2\theta
Unpolarized I_0 through two Polaroids at \theta (I_0/2)\cos^2\theta
Two Polaroids crossed (\theta = 90^{\circ}) zero
Three sheets, first and third crossed, middle at 45° (I_0/2)(\cos^2 45^{\circ})(\cos^2 45^{\circ}) = I_0/8

One sheet halves, it does not pass

Unpolarized light through a single Polaroid comes out at half intensity, not at full intensity: the sheet removes the component perpendicular to its axis.

Students who forget the factor 1/2 get twice the right answer for every stacked-sheet question. And a crossed pair gives zero no matter how bright the source is.

Worked example 13.8 — two Polaroids at 60°

Problem. Unpolarized light of intensity I_0 passes through two Polaroids whose axes are at 60° to each other. Find the emergent intensity.

Solution. The first sheet halves it: I_0/2. Malus then gives (I_0/2)\cos^2 60^{\circ} = (I_0/2)(1/4) = I_0/8. The answer I_0/4 comes from forgetting the halving; 3I_0/8 from using \sin^2 instead of \cos^2.

13.3.4 Polarization by reflection: Brewster's law

When unpolarized light strikes a transparent surface, both the reflected and the refracted beams are partially polarized.

At one particular angle of incidence — the polarizing angle or Brewster angle \theta_p — the reflected beam is completely plane-polarized, with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence. Brewster found that

\tan\theta_p = \mu

where \mu is the refractive index of the reflecting medium relative to the medium the light comes from. At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are at right angles:

\theta_p + r = 90^{\circ}

Medium (from air) \mu \theta_p
Water 1.33 53°
Glass 1.50 56.3°
A medium with \mu = \sqrt{3} 1.732 60°
Worked example 13.9 — Brewster angle and the refracted ray

Problem. Light is incident from air on a medium of refractive index \sqrt{3}. Find the polarizing angle and the angle of refraction.

Solution. \tan\theta_p = \sqrt{3}, so \theta_p = 60^{\circ}. Then r = 90^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 30^{\circ}.

Check with Snell's law \sin 60^{\circ}/\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.866/0.5 = 1.732 = \sqrt{3}. ✓

13.3.5 Why reflected light is partially polarized

The reflected beam is the radiation of the electric dipoles that the incident wave sets oscillating in the medium. A dipole does not radiate along its own axis of oscillation.

  • Dipoles oscillating perpendicular to the plane of incidence (parallel to the surface) can always radiate back into the reflected direction.
  • Dipoles oscillating in the plane of incidence cannot radiate along their axis. At the Brewster angle the refracted ray is at 90° to the reflected ray, so those dipoles point exactly along the direction in which the reflected beam would travel — and they radiate nothing into it.

So at \theta_p only the perpendicular component is reflected: the reflected beam is 100 % polarized. At any other angle the in-plane component is only partly suppressed, so the reflected beam is partially polarized.

The refracted beam is also partially polarized, but in the complementary sense (it is richer in the in-plane component).

13.3.6 Where polarization is used

  • Sunglasses. Glare from a horizontal road or water surface is largely horizontally polarized; a Polaroid with a vertical transmission axis blocks it while passing about half of the rest of the scene.
  • Photography. A rotating polarizing filter removes reflections from glass and water and darkens the sky, because scattered skylight is polarized.
  • Liquid-crystal displays work by switching the polarization of light between crossed polaroids.
  • 3-D cinema projects two images with perpendicular polarizations, and each eyepiece passes only one.
  • Stress analysis in transparent models, and the study of optically active substances (a sugar solution rotates the plane of polarization).

Formula and fact sheet

Topic Formula or fact
Superposition I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi
Phase from path \phi = 2\pi\Delta/\lambda
Bright / dark \Delta = n\lambda / \Delta = (2n-1)\lambda/2
Amplitude and intensity I \propto a^2; equal sources: I_{max} = 4I_0, I_{min} = 0
Intensity ratio I_{max}/I_{min} = (a_1+a_2)^2/(a_1-a_2)^2
Visibility V = (I_{max}-I_{min})/(I_{max}+I_{min})
YDSE bright y_n = n\lambda D/d
YDSE dark y_n = (2n-1)\lambda D/d
Fringe width \beta = \lambda D/d; in a medium \beta/\mu; angular width \lambda/d
Slab in one path shift = (\mu-1)t/\beta fringes, towards the slab
Thin film, reflected 2\mu t\cos r + \lambda/2 = n\lambda (bright), = (2n-1)\lambda/2 (dark)
Anti-reflection coating t = \lambda/(4\mu)
Newton's rings dark r_n = \sqrt{n\lambda R}; bright r_n = \sqrt{(2n-1)\lambda R/2}; centre dark in reflection
Single-slit minima a\sin\theta = n\lambda
Single-slit secondary maxima a\sin\theta \approx (2n+1)\lambda/2
Central maximum width 2D\lambda/a; secondary maximum D\lambda/a
Grating (a+b)\sin\theta = n\lambda; d = 1/N; n_{max} = d/\lambda
Grating resolving power nN
Telescope \theta_{min} = 1.22\lambda/D; RP = D/(1.22\lambda)
Microscope d_{min} = \lambda/(2\mu\sin\theta); RP = 2\mu\sin\theta/\lambda
Malus I = I_0\cos^2\theta; one Polaroid halves unpolarized light
Brewster \tan\theta_p = \mu; \theta_p + r = 90^{\circ}
Standard values glass \mu = 1.5, \theta_p \approx 56.3^{\circ}; water \mu = 4/3, \theta_p \approx 53^{\circ}

Chapter summary

  • Interference is superposition of coherent waves; intensity is I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi with \phi = 2\pi\Delta/\lambda. Equal sources give 4I_0 bright and zero dark.
  • Bright fringes need \Delta = n\lambda; dark fringes need \Delta = (2n-1)\lambda/2. Optical path is \mu times geometrical path.
  • Coherent beams are made by dividing a wavefront (double slit) or an amplitude (thin film). Two independent lamps never interfere.
  • Young's double slit: y_n = n\lambda D/d for bright fringes and \beta = \lambda D/d for the spacing — independent of the order, proportional to \lambda and D, inversely proportional to d, and divided by \mu in a liquid.
  • A slab of thickness t shifts the whole pattern by (\mu-1)t/\beta fringes towards the covered slit without changing \beta.
  • In a thin film the reflected beams differ by 2\mu t\cos r + \lambda/2; in Newton's rings the reflected centre is dark and r_n = \sqrt{n\lambda R} for dark rings.
  • Single slit: minima at a\sin\theta = n\lambda, central maximum of width 2D\lambda/a, twice the width of the secondary maxima.
  • Grating: (a+b)\sin\theta = n\lambda; highest order n_{max} = d/\lambda; the maxima are sharp because many slits contribute.
  • Resolving power: telescope D/(1.22\lambda), microscope 2\mu\sin\theta/\lambda — bigger aperture or higher refractive index resolves finer detail.
  • Polarization proves light is transverse. Malus: I = I_0\cos^2\theta, with one Polaroid halving unpolarized light. Brewster: \tan\theta_p = \mu, and at that angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular and the reflected beam is fully polarized.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — coherence means a fixed phase relationship, which requires the same frequency. Equal amplitude or equal intensity alone gives no stable pattern.

2. (b) — \beta = \lambda D/d. Option (a) is the reciprocal arrangement and (c) is the central-maximum width of a single slit.

3. (d) — constructive interference needs a whole number of wavelengths, \Delta = n\lambda; (2n-1)\lambda/2 is the destructive condition.

4. (a) — one wavelength is one full cycle, so \phi = 2\pi\Delta/\lambda = 2\pi.

5. (b) — in water \lambda falls to \lambda/\mu, and \beta \propto \lambda, so the fringes get closer together.

6. (c) — pairing the slit into halves gives \frac{a}{2}\sin\theta = \lambda/2, hence a\sin\theta = \lambda. (a) is the double-slit path-difference condition misapplied.

7. (a) — the first minimum is at y = \lambda D/a, and the central maximum extends symmetrically to both sides, so its full width is 2\lambda D/a.

8. (d) — the path difference between neighbouring slits is (a+b)\sin\theta, set equal to n\lambda for a maximum.

9. (c) — resolving power is the reciprocal of the angular limit 1.22\lambda/D. Option (a) is the limit of resolution itself, not the power.

10. (b) — the transmitted amplitude is a_0\cos\theta, so the intensity is I_0\cos^2\theta.

11. (a) — \tan\theta_p = \mu. At this angle \theta_p + r = 90^{\circ}.

12. (d) — the two rays are perpendicular at the polarizing angle; this is what allows the dipoles to radiate nothing into the reflected direction.

13. (c) — each atom emits a train of about 10^{-8} s with random phase, so the phase difference is not constant.

14. (b) — \beta = \lambda D/d, so \beta \propto \lambda. Frequency is inversely related to wavelength, so (c) is wrong.

15. (d) — a Polaroid absorbs the component along its aligned molecules and transmits the perpendicular one: selective absorption.

16. (a) — at the centre the air film has zero thickness, which satisfies the dark condition, so the centre is dark.

17. (c) — amplitudes add to 2a, and intensity goes as amplitude squared: 4I_0.

18. (b) — the angle subtended at the slits by one fringe is \beta/D = \lambda/d.

19. (d) — the nth dark fringe needs \Delta = (2n-1)\lambda/2; with n = 3 this is 5\lambda/2.

20. (a) — diffraction is strong only when the obstacle or aperture is of the order of a wavelength.

21. (c) — only transverse waves can be polarized, so polarization proves light is transverse. Interference and diffraction occur for longitudinal waves too.

22. (b) — the grating element is the slit spacing, d = 1/N when N is in lines per metre.

23. (d) — all wavelengths have zero path difference at the centre, so all colours arrive in phase and the central fringe is white.

24. (a) — \beta = \lambda D/d contains no n; every fringe is the same distance from the next.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Describe Young's double-slit experiment and derive the fringe width. State the conditions for sustained interference. [10]
  2. Explain single-slit diffraction, the diffraction grating, and polarisation with Brewster's and Malus' laws. [10]

Model answer D1: Young's double-slit experiment (10 marks)

Introduction. Interference is the redistribution of energy when two coherent waves overlap. It supports the wave nature of light.

Young obtained two coherent sources by dividing one wavefront with two narrow slits S_1 and S_2 separated by d, with the screen at a distance D.

Derivation. A point P at a distance y from the central point O receives waves from both slits. The path difference is \Delta = S_2P - S_1P \approx \dfrac{yd}{D} for d, y \ll D.

  1. Bright fringe: \Delta = n\lambda, so y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}, with n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
  2. Dark fringe: \Delta = (n + \tfrac12)\lambda, so y_n = \dfrac{(n + \tfrac12)\lambda D}{d}.
  3. Fringe width (distance between consecutive bright or dark fringes): \beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}.
  4. Intensity. With equal slits, I = 4I_0\cos^2\dfrac\phi2, where \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta is the phase difference. I_{max} = 4I_0, I_{min} = 0, and the average is 2I_0, so energy is conserved.

Conditions for sustained interference. The two sources must be coherent (constant phase difference), of the same frequency, have nearly equal amplitudes for good contrast, and be close together. The slits must be narrow and the screen far away.

Change Effect on fringe width
Blue light instead of red decreases (\lambda smaller)
Slit separation doubled halves
Screen moved farther increases
Whole set-up in water decreases by factor n
Thin sheet of thickness t over one slit pattern shifts by (n - 1)tD/d, width unchanged

White light gives a white central fringe with coloured edges on both sides.

Numerical. For \lambda = 600\ \text{nm}, d = 0.5\ \text{mm} and D = 1.5\ \text{m}: \beta = \dfrac{600\times10^{-9}\times1.5}{0.5\times10^{-3}} = 1.8\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 1.8\ \text{mm}.

The third bright fringe is at 3\times1.8 = 5.4\ \text{mm} and the second dark fringe at 1.5\times1.8 = 2.7\ \text{mm}.

Conclusion. Fringe width \beta = \lambda D/d is uniform, and the experiment gives a simple way to measure the wavelength of light.

Model answer D2: diffraction, grating and polarisation (10 marks)

Introduction. Diffraction is the bending of waves around obstacles or through openings of size comparable to the wavelength.

Single slit (width a). The minima are at a\sin\theta = n\lambda (n = \pm1, \pm2, \ldots), and the central maximum, twice as wide as the others, has width \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a} on the screen. Narrower slits give a wider pattern.

The secondary maxima are much weaker (about 4.5\% and 1.6\% of the central one).

Diffraction grating. A grating has many equally spaced slits with spacing d = 1/N (N lines per metre). The principal maxima obey d\sin\theta = n\lambda. The maxima are sharp, so the grating separates wavelengths far better than a prism.

The maximum order is n_{max} < d/\lambda.

Polarisation. Light is a transverse wave, so it can be polarised. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be.

  1. Malus' law. The intensity transmitted by an analyser at angle \theta to the polariser is I = I_0\cos^2\theta. An unpolarised beam falls to half its intensity on passing a polariser.
  2. Brewster's law. At the polarising angle \theta_p, the reflected light is completely plane-polarised and \tan\theta_p = n. The reflected and refracted rays are then at 90^{\circ}.
  3. Uses. Sunglasses, 3-D cinema, stress analysis in glass, and sugar solution analysis (optical activity).
Feature Interference Diffraction
Sources two coherent sources single wavefront, many points
Fringes equal width unequal width
Intensity of minima zero not exactly zero

Numerical.

  • A slit of width 0.1\ \text{mm} with \lambda = 500\ \text{nm} and D = 1\ \text{m} gives a central maximum of width \dfrac{2\times5\times10^{-7}\times1}{10^{-4}} = 1\ \text{cm}.
  • A grating with 5000 lines per cm has d = 2\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}. For 500\ \text{nm}, \sin\theta_1 = 0.25, \theta_1 = 14.5^{\circ}, and d/\lambda = 4, so the highest order is 3 (the fourth falls at 90^{\circ}). Total number of maxima = 7.
  • For glass with n = 1.5, \theta_p = \tan^{-1}1.5 = 56.3^{\circ}. An unpolarised beam of intensity 100 passes two polarisers at 60^{\circ} to each other: 100\times\tfrac12\times\cos^260^{\circ} = 12.5.

Conclusion. Diffraction limits the resolution of instruments, the grating exploits it to analyse light, and polarisation proves that light is transverse.
